chunks.text: Gulmohar (Delonix regia), also called the flame tree, royal poinciana or flamboyant, is a flowering tree in the bean family Fabaceae. It is endemic to the dry deciduous forests of Madagascar, where its wild population was not discovered until 1932 and where it is now endangered in the wild, even though it has been cultivated and naturalised across the tropics and subtropics for centuries — including throughout India, Southeast Asia, Africa, the Americas and the Mediterranean. It is a medium-sized deciduous tree, usually reaching about 5-12 metres, with light brown, lenticelled bark and feathery, doubly pinnate leaves 30-50 cm long made up of 20-40 pairs of leaflets. Its showy flowers have four spreading scarlet or orange-red petals up to 8-11 cm across plus a larger, yellow-and-white-spotted fifth petal; a rare naturally-occurring yellow-flowered variety also exists. In India, the tree is typically bare from December to February, leafs out in March-April and flowers in April-May, with the long, dark, woody seed pods (up to 60 cm) persisting on the tree well after that.

chunks.source: Wikipedia — Delonix regia (ornamental use and cultural significance)
chunks.text: Delonix regia is grown almost entirely as an ornamental and shade tree, valued for its dense canopy and spectacular flowering rather than for timber, food or medicine; it tolerates drought and salty conditions but needs free-draining, tropical or near-tropical growing conditions. It is the state tree of Delhi and the national flower of St Kitts and Nevis, and among Kerala's Saint Thomas Christian community it carries an association with Calvary. In Vietnam, where it is called 'phượng vĩ,' its flowering coincides with the end of the school year and it is known as the 'pupil's flower'; in the Philippines its bloom signals the start of the monsoon, and in Myanmar it marks the Thingyan festival. Despite being endangered in its native Madagascar habitat, it is rated Least Concern globally on the IUCN Red List because of how widely it has been planted elsewhere.
